title: UNIQUE & CHECK Constraints
description: Guarantee distinctness with UNIQUE constraints, enforce business logic with CHECK expressions, and handle multiple NULLs.

data.text: **UNIQUE** constraints prevent duplicate non-null entries in one or more columns, automatically backing them with a B-tree index. **CHECK** constraints validate column values against arbitrary boolean expressions before allowing writes.
UNIQUE NULL Handling (UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT in PG 15+)

Historically in SQL, `NULL` values are treated as distinct; thus, a standard `UNIQUE` column can hold multiple `NULL` rows. In PostgreSQL 15+, you can specify `UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT` to enforce that only a single `NULL` is permitted.

data.title: CHECK Constraint with Business Rules
data.content: Validating that price is positive and discounted price is lower than list price.
data.code:
CREATE TABLE products (
    id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    price NUMERIC(10, 2) NOT NULL,
    sale_price NUMERIC(10, 2),
    CONSTRAINT chk_price_positive CHECK (price > 0),
    CONSTRAINT chk_sale_lower_than_price CHECK (sale_price IS NULL OR sale_price < price)
);

data.text: In SQL, `NULL` means "unknown", and two unknowns are not equal. A standard `UNIQUE` constraint therefore permits many rows whose constrained columns are `NULL`. PostgreSQL 15 added `NULLS NOT DISTINCT` to invert that behaviour when a single `NULL` should be allowed.

data.title: Both Behaviours, Side by Side
data.content: This is a very common interview question.

data.text: A plain `UNIQUE` constraint is really a unique **index**. Once you see it that way, you can express conditions that a naive constraint cannot: unique only among active rows, unique on a derived value, or unique on a combination.

data.title: Conditional and Derived Uniqueness
data.content: Partial unique indexes solve the "one active record per user" problem.

data.text: CHECK Constraints: What They Can and Cannot Do

items: They can reference any column in the same row, use functions marked `IMMUTABLE`/`STABLE`, and use `CASE`, `regex` (`~`), and `ANY`/`ALL` with arrays.
They **cannot** reference other rows or other tables — that needs a foreign key, an exclusion constraint, or a trigger.
They are evaluated on `INSERT` and `UPDATE` only; a `CHECK` that is true today stays stored even if the expression would now be false.
A `CHECK` that evaluates to `NULL` passes, because `NULL` is not `false`. Guard with `col IS NOT NULL OR ...` when that matters.

data.title: CHECK Constraints With Real Business Rules
data.code:
CREATE TABLE bookings (
    id         BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    check_in   DATE NOT NULL,
    check_out  DATE NOT NULL,
    guests     SMALLINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
    status     TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending',

    CONSTRAINT dates_ordered   CHECK (check_out > check_in),
    CONSTRAINT stay_not_absurd CHECK (check_out - check_in <= 365),
    CONSTRAINT guests_positive CHECK (guests BETWEEN 1 AND 20),
    CONSTRAINT known_status    CHECK (status IN ('pending','confirmed','cancelled')),
    -- NULL passes a check: make the intent explicit
    CONSTRAINT cancel_reason   CHECK (status <> 'cancelled' OR cancelled_reason IS NOT NULL)
);

INSERT INTO bookings (check_in, check_out, guests)
VALUES ('2026-05-01','2026-05-04', 2);

INSERT INTO bookings (check_in, check_out) VALUES ('2026-05-04','2026-05-01');
-- ERROR: new row for relation "bookings" violates check constraint "dates_ordered"

data.title: Interview Answer
data.text: If asked "does `UNIQUE` allow multiple `NULL`s?", say yes, because `NULL` is not equal to `NULL` — and mention `UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT` (PG 15+) and partial unique indexes as the two ways to get stricter behaviour.

data.title: Constrain a Subscription Table
steps: Create `subscriptions(user_id, plan, started_at, cancelled_at)` with `plan` restricted to a known set.
Add a check that `cancelled_at` is `NULL` or after `started_at`.
Add a partial unique index so each user has at most one active (not cancelled) subscription.
Prove both rules with failing inserts.
data.expectedOutcome: A schema where invalid subscription states are impossible to store.

items.question: When should a rule live in the database instead of the application?
items.answer: When it is a true invariant: uniqueness, referential integrity, and domain ranges. Database constraints hold under concurrent writes, background jobs, and manual fixes — application code cannot.

items.question: Does a `CHECK` constraint slow down inserts?
items.answer: Marginally. The expression is evaluated per modified row; for cheap expressions the cost is negligible compared to the surrounding I/O.

items.question: Can I add a `CHECK` constraint without scanning the table?
items.answer: Yes: `ADD CONSTRAINT ... CHECK (...) NOT VALID;` skips validation, then `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT` verifies existing rows with a lighter lock.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: `UNIQUE` constraints automatically generate an underlying B-tree index.
Use `CHECK` constraints to enforce business domain rules directly in the database.
Use `NULLS NOT DISTINCT` (PG 15+) when you want unique constraints to reject duplicate NULLs.
